title: The song of bliss
hookLine: tradition links his great hymn, the Anand Sahib, to joy at a grandson's birth; it is sung at every ceremony

cards: Good news has a way of tumbling out before the hello is over. Mom, guess what. Guru Amar Das was an old man by now.

Tradition says a grandson was born to his son, Mohri, and the family was full of joy. The baby was named Anand. Around that time, tradition says, the Guru composed a hymn Sikhs still sing at every turn of life.
It opens, in effect, with that same rush of good news, told to a mother.

teach.b: It's called the Anand Sahib, the song of bliss. Anand means bliss, deep joy, the kind that settles in rather than flashing past. The hymn has forty stanzas, in raga Ramkali.

teach.h: I AM IN BLISS, O MY MOTHER.
teach.b: Its first line goes something like this, in paraphrase: I am in bliss, O my mother, for I have found my true Guru. Notice who hears the news first: mother, the one who has known the singer longest.
And the news isn't wealth or success.

teach.h: THE NEWS: I'VE FOUND THE TRUE GURU.
teach.b: The singer has found the true Guru, and the mind is at peace. The hymn says this bliss can't be bought or faked; it comes through the Guru's word, and it sings of the Word ringing inside like music.
Tradition links the hymn to the grandson's birth, and the child and the hymn share a name. You may have heard it without knowing.
The Anand Sahib, or its opening stanzas and last stanza, is sung at Sikh ceremonies of every kind: a wedding, a baby's naming, the end of the congregation's prayers, even a funeral.
Joy, on this path, isn't only for happy days.

It's the steady bliss of being close to the Guru, and it holds even when life is sad. Those same stanzas are part of Rehras, the Sikh evening prayer. A song that began with a family's joy now closes Sikh gatherings.

how: The Anand Sahib is part of the Sikh daily prayers, and its first five stanzas with the fortieth are sung at the close of congregational worship and at weddings, namings and funerals.

games.q: you're writing a hymn about finding the deepest joy of your life. who do you tell first?
games.why: the Anand Sahib opens by telling a mother: I am in bliss, for I have found my true Guru.

practice: Sing or hum something joyful: a lullaby, a hymn from your childhood, a song from a wedding you loved. Nobody's listening, and it doesn't have to be good; let your chest buzz with it.
If gladness comes, let it stay a moment, and if it doesn't, just keep the tune going.

wordCard.voice: Anand. Bliss, deep joy; the name of Guru Amar Das's grandson, and of the hymn that closes Sikh ceremonies. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: anand, bliss; the Anand Sahib, and the Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding, share the word.
